extracted.intended_audience: patent drafters, patent attorneys, and applicants preparing patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing patent applications and drafting claims: what parts to include in an application, how to draft the description and drawings, and fundamental principles and formats for claim drafting (preambles, transitional phrases, bodies, grammar, and strategy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Request (application form) contents
rubrics_metrics.description: The request explicitly states that an applicant seeks patent protection and is signed by the applicant or its representative. The request form will generally contain: the title of the invention; the name and address of the applicant and their representative; an indication of the inventor; and information relating to the priority claim, such as the application number and filing date of the earlier application on which the priority is based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each patent office provides a specific request form; all priority information should be included in the patent application, whether on the request form or in an application data sheet. In the United States, related applications may be described under “CROSS-REFERENCE TO RELATED APPLICATION.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Description: sufficiency and completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: The description discloses the invention sufficiently clearly and completely to the extent that a person skilled in the art will be able to carry out the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To improve readability, the description usually contains sections: title, technical field, background art, summary of the invention, brief explanation of the drawings, and detailed disclosure by way of examples (embodiments). Examples/embodiments often play an important role in meeting the support requirement and the enablement requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims define scope and determine patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: The claims define the scope of exclusive patent protection in terms of the technical features of the invention; they are the legally operative part of a patent application and whether an invention meets patentability requirements is determined on the basis of the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must be clear and concise, as well as fully supported by the description. The claims are typically the first portion examined by interested parties and examiners; therefore clarity is of the utmost importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings as visual support
rubrics_metrics.description: The drawings provide visual support in describing the invention and often facilitate better understanding of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawings may include figures, tables, flow charts and diagrams; a representative drawing is usually positioned on the front page of a published patent document.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract: concise searchable summary
rubrics_metrics.description: The abstract is a summary (a digest) of the invention limited to a certain number of words; it typically includes key features recited in the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The abstract primarily aids patent searches and gives an overview to readers of patent documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application format and jurisdictional variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the five main parts are common across many countries and under the PCT, their detailed format is rarely the same; section headings may differ between jurisdictions and some offices supply sample application forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Common Application Format (CAF) exists (accepted by EPO, JPO, KIPO, CNIPA and USPTO) to standardize headings and order of sections, reducing burden when applying across territories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include all priority information
rubrics_metrics.description: All priority information, such as the information about the earlier application on which priority is claimed or information about the parent application in a divisional, should be included in the patent application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Priority details can be placed on the request form or in an application data sheet; timely and accurate priority disclosure is essential for claiming Paris Convention rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention vs embodiment vs claims
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is a construct inside the mind of the inventor; an embodiment is a physical form of the invention; the claims must protect at least an embodiment of the invention but the best claims protect the invention itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims do not define the invention but are a written approximation; patent drafters should aim to claim the invention broadly (not just specific embodiments) so others cannot practice the inventive concept without infringing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support requirement: claims must be supported by the description
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be supported by the description; terminology used in claims should track through the description consistently and every claim must be adequately supported in the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim not supported by the description can be thrown out. In jurisdictions with strict support (e.g., EPO), the description must specifically include at least one embodiment that explicitly demonstrates the claimed combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim breadth strategy (broad and narrow claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent drafters should aim at a broad set of claims that covers various aspects of the invention at various levels of detail while also including narrower claims as fallbacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because prior art is unpredictable, include a range of claims from broad to narrow; narrower claims can survive if broad claims are invalidated. Drafting strategy complexity is acknowledged and further treated in Module VI.

rubrics_metrics.name: All-elements rule for infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: To assert patent infringement, all of the elements of a claim must be reproduced in the third party's accused embodiment (element-by-element comparison).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If any claimed element is missing or altered (e.g., light attached to center vs end), there is no infringement. The term 'element' is synonymous with technical feature or limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of claim elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims may include different kinds of elements: structural, functional, relational, intentional, parametric and activity elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: structural ('a screw'), functional ('fastening means'), relational ('attached'), intentional ('for treating cancer'), parametric (measurable properties), activity (process steps in gerund form). Choose element types appropriate to the subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim format conventions (sentence, tense, punctuation, numbering)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is traditionally written as a single sentence and in the present tense. Each claim begins with a capital letter and ends with a period. Claims are numbered consecutively and all claims appear in a separate 'Claims' section clearly separated from other parts of the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Periods are usually not used elsewhere except in abbreviations; semicolons separate clauses/phrases; many offices accept or require line indentation for elements. Follow punctuation conventions (comma between preamble and transitional phrase; colon before body; elements separated by semicolons with penultimate element followed by '; and').

rubrics_metrics.name: Parts of a claim: preamble, transitional phrase, body
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is generally in three parts – the preamble (identifies category), the transitional phrase (open or closed), and the body (recites elements and relationships).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure each part is chosen carefully: the preamble's breadth affects scope, transitional phrase choice (open vs closed) impacts inclusivity, and the body must interrelate elements rather than merely list them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble breadth and drafting considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: The preamble identifies the category of the invention (apparatus, method, composition, etc.) and may include premodifiers/postmodifiers; more adjectives or complements narrow the scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the preamble at the right level of breadth; broader preambles may invite unity/divisional objections; preamble weight in litigation varies by jurisdiction—assess whether preamble 'breathes life' into the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional phrases: open-ended vs closed
rubrics_metrics.description: Open-ended phrases (e.g., 'comprising', 'including') are inclusive and do not exclude additional elements; closed phrases ('consisting of') limit the claim to only the recited elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use open-ended phrases to allow additional elements; closed phrases make avoidance easier for infringers. Jurisdictional interpretations vary (e.g., 'comprising' may be treated narrowly in Australia). Professional tip: prefer amending claims to avoid prior art rather than relying on closed transitional phrases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body of claim must interrelate elements (not mere list)
rubrics_metrics.description: The body recites the elements and explains how they exist in relationship to one another; a claim cannot be merely a list of parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Connect elements logically (e.g., 'a top configured to be supported by at least one leg'). Many patent offices will reject claims that are simple unconnected lists of parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper antecedent basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements in a claim must demonstrate correct antecedent basis: introduce an element with 'a' or 'an' on first use and refer back with 'the'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each new claim set must re-establish antecedent basis. 'The' and 'said' are interchangeable, though 'said' is old-fashioned; plain language is trending. To refer to multiple distinct elements, use 'first'/'second' or 'another' to avoid ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference numerals and parenthetical expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: In some jurisdictions, claims are encouraged or required to recite reference numerals that correspond to drawings; for PCT applications they shall preferably appear in parentheses after corresponding elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference numerals aid comprehension by linking claims to drawings but are generally not to be interpreted as limiting the claim scope; the drafter may comment in the description to that effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripheral claiming doctrine and drafting implication
rubrics_metrics.description: Most countries follow a 'peripheral claiming' doctrine in which the claims establish the outer limits of patent protection; thus drafting claims to set the limits of protection sought is critical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless filing in a jurisdiction that allows 'central claiming', draft claims to define the outer limits of protection. Consider how claim wording will be interpreted by examiners and courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation and grammatical detail are substantive
rubrics_metrics.description: Many patent offices stipulate requirements for punctuation and formatting; claims are frequently more extensively punctuated than grammatically required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use commas, colons, semi-colons and line indentation as appropriate to make the claim's intended structure clear. Failure to attend to punctuation/grammar may lead to rejections even for substantively sound claims.
